title: The effect of niacinamide on reducing cutaneous pigmentation and suppression of melanosome transfer
raw_title: The effect of niacinamide on reducing cutaneous pigmentation and suppression of melanosome transfer
authors: Hakozaki T; Minwalla L; Zhuang J; Chhoa M; Matsubara A; Miyamoto K; Greatens A; Hillebrand GG; Bissett DL; Boissy RE
population: Japanese women with facial hyperpigmentation (n=18) or facial tanning (n=120)
funding_or_conflicts: Not extracted from abstract; check full-text disclosures.
limitations: Asian population only; phototypes not reported in abstract; moisturiser vehicle; full-text effect sizes not extracted.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): In vitro: no effect on tyrosinase or melanocyte melanogenesis; reduced melanosome transfer in co-culture. title: A comparative study of 20% azelaic acid cream monotherapy versus a sequential therapy in the treatment of melasma in dark-skinned patients
raw_title: A comparative study of 20% azelaic acid cream monotherapy versus sequential therapy in dark-skinned patients
authors: Sarkar R; Bhalla M; Kanwar AJ
population: 30 Indian patients with melasma (25 female; 5 male) completed
limitations: No vehicle control: both arms received azelaic acid; cannot isolate azelaic acid efficacy; small sample; phototypes not reported in abstract.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Sequential potent topical steroid then 20% azelaic acid lightened melasma significantly more at 4/8/16 weeks than 20% azelaic acid alone. || Verification sources: https://search.worldcat.org/title/4815918399?oclcNum=4815918399 ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.2165/00128071-200405010-00011

title: Topical 5% tranexamic acid for the treatment of melasma in Asians: a double-blind randomized controlled clinical trial
raw_title: Topical 5% tranexamic acid for treatment of melasma in Asians: double-blind randomized trial
authors: Kanechorn Na Ayuthaya P; et al. (full list to confirm)
journal: Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy
population: Thai patients with melasma (Phramongkutklao Hospital; Chiang Mai University)
limitations: Vehicle-controlled but null between-arm result; sample size and phototypes not confirmed from abstract.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Split-face 5% tranexamic acid vs vehicle with sunscreen: lightening occurred on both sides; difference between regimens NOT statistically significant; tranexamic acid caused erythema. || Verification sources: https://read.qxmd.com/read/22506692/topical-5-tranexamic-acid-for-the-treatment-of-melasma-in-asians-a-double-blind-randomized-controlled-clinical-trial ; https://data.zhenzhi.com/details/1/867810573

title: A double-blind randomized trial of 5% ascorbic acid vs. 4% hydroquinone in melasma
raw_title: Double-blind randomized trial of 5% ascorbic acid vs 4% hydroquinone in melasma
authors: Espinal-Perez LE; Moncada B; Castanedo-Cazares JP
population: 16 women with idiopathic melasma
limitations: Very small; no vehicle arm (active comparator only); phototypes not reported in abstract.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Split-face, 16 weeks: hydroquinone better (93% vs 62.5% good/excellent subjective improvement); side effects 68.7% with hydroquinone vs 6.2% with ascorbic acid. || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15304189/ ; https://katalog.lib.cas.cz/KNAV/EdsRecord/edsair,edsair.doi.dedup.....871a45bb38b9f5d2e7855cdf4244cf62

title: The safety and efficacy of salicylic acid chemical peels in darker racial-ethnic groups
raw_title: The safety and efficacy of salicylic acid chemical peels in darker racial-ethnic groups
authors: Grimes PE
population: 25 patients, skin types V-VI (acne 9, PIH 5, melasma 6, oily/rough skin 5)
limitations: Uncontrolled pilot; peel concentrations (20-30%) are not leave-on cosmetic use; hydroquinone co-treatment confounds pigment outcomes.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): After 2 weeks of 4% hydroquinone pre-treatment, five 20-30% salicylic acid peels at 2-week intervals: moderate-to-significant improvement in 88%; minimal-to-mild side effects. || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9935087/ ; https://data.zhenzhi.com/details/1/874773060

title: Glycolic acid peels for postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in black patients. A comparative study
raw_title: Glycolic acid peels for postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in Black patients: comparative study
authors: Burns RL; Prevost-Blank PL; Lawry MA; Lawry TB; Faria DT; Fivenson DP
population: 19 patients, Fitzpatrick IV-VI, randomised (16 completed)
limitations: Pilot; trend not clearly significant; both arms received glycolic acid and hydroquinone/tretinoin; peel strength is not leave-on cosmetic use.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Both arms used 2% hydroquinone/10% glycolic acid gel + 0.05% tretinoin; peel arm added six serial glycolic acid peels (up to 68%). Both improved; peel arm showed a trend toward faster and greater improvement; peels also lightened normal skin. || Verification sources: https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9145958 ; https://www.curehunter.com/public/pubmed9145958.do

title: Topical treatments for melasma and their mechanism of action
raw_title: Topical treatments for melasma and their mechanism of action: systematic review
authors: González-Molina V; Martí-Pineda A; González N
journal: Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology
population: Review of published melasma studies (PubMed only; PRISMA)
limitations: Single-database search; not an isolated lactic-acid trial: category context only.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Review of topical melasma agents; concludes hydroquinone remains the comparator standard; tranexamic acid and cysteamine as adjuvant/maintenance options. || Verification sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9122278/ ; https://jcadonline.com/topical-treatments-melasma-mechanism-of-action/

title: The efficacy of topical cosmetic containing alpha-arbutin 5% and kojic acid 2% compared with triple combination cream for the treatment of melasma: a split-face evaluator-blinded randomized pilot study
raw_title: Topical alpha-arbutin 5% and kojic acid 2% vs triple combination for melasma
authors: Tantanasrigul P; Sripha A; Chongmelaxme B
population: 30 adults with facial melasma randomised split-face (Thailand); 27 analysed per trade press
limitations: Pilot; combination product so no isolated alpha-arbutin effect; 5% alpha-arbutin exceeds the EU 2% face-cream limit; PMID taken from raw file and not independently confirmed (PMC11740261 confirmed).
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 12 weeks + 4-week follow-up: hemi-mMASI and melanin index not statistically different between alpha-arbutin 5% + kojic acid 2% and triple combination cream; physician global assessment favoured triple combination; fewer adverse events with the cosmetic. || Verification sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11740261/ ; https://trial.medpath.com/clinical-trial/23bb83fdc9623055/topical-cosmetic-melasma-treatment

title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
raw_title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
authors: Kafi R; Kwak HSR; Schumacher WE; Cho S; Hanft VN; Hamilton TA; King AL; Neal JD; Varani J; Fisher GJ; Voorhees JJ; Kang S
population: 36 adults aged 80+ (mean 87); upper inner arm, naturally aged (sun-protected) skin
funding_or_conflicts: NIH and non-US government support (PubMed); registered NCT00272610.
limitations: Elderly, arm skin, not facial photoageing; 0.4% exceeds the EU 0.3% retinol-equivalent limit for face products and the 0.05% body-lotion limit; mild irritation common.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 0.4% retinol lotion vs vehicle, left/right arm, up to 3x weekly for 24 weeks: fine-wrinkle score change -1.64 (95% CI -2.06 to -1.22) vs -0.08 (P<.001); increased glycosaminoglycan and procollagen I in biopsy subgroups. || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17515510/ ; https://pure.johnshopkins.edu/en/publications/improvement-of-naturally-aged-skin-with-vitamin-a-retinol-4/

title: Thiamidol in moderate-to-severe melasma: 24-week, randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled clinical study with subsequent regression phase
raw_title: Thiamidol in moderate-to-severe melasma: randomized double-blind trial in phototypes III–V
authors: Roggenkamp D; Sammain A; Fürstenau M; Kausch M; Passeron T; Kolbe L
population: Moderate-to-severe melasma; phototypes III-V

notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Clinical photography and MASI improved with Thiamidol vs baseline (p<0.001) and vs vehicle (p<0.001-0.043), followed by a regression phase. || Verification sources: https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/bvsiec/resource/pt/mdl-34676600 ; https://www.practiceupdate.com/content/thiamidol-improves-melasma-but-may-not-be-superior-to-sun-protection-alone/126546

title: Effect of a ceramide NP-containing moisturizer on skin barrier function in adults with atopic dermatitis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
raw_title: Effect of a Ceramide NP-containing moisturizer on barrier function: randomized trial
population: 60 adults with moderate atopic dermatitis (single centre)
limitations: Finished product: cannot attribute to Ceramide NP alone; between-group significance and author list not confirmed from accessible text.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Emollient cream with ceramide NP vs placebo alongside standard therapy, assessed at days 21 and 42: barrier parameters improved in both arms with 'more favorable numerical trends' in the intervention arm; between-group results to be extracted. || Author list not confirmed from accessible sources. || Verification sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13722463 ; https://karger.com/spp/online-first

title: A daily regimen of a ceramide-dominant moisturizing cream and cleanser restores the skin permeability barrier in adults with moderate eczema: a randomized trial
raw_title: Ceramide-dominant moisturizer randomized trial
authors: Spada F; Harrison IP; Barnes TM; Greive KA; Daniels D; Townley JP; Mostafa N; Fong AT; Tong PL; Shumack S
population: Adults with moderate eczema (single centre; Australia)
funding_or_conflicts: Products from Ego Pharmaceuticals; author affiliations to be checked in full text.
limitations: Finished two-product regimen (QV Intensive with Ceramides): cannot attribute to any single ceramide species; products supplied by the manufacturer.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Ceramide cream + cleanser vs placebo, 28 days: EASI improved in both arms, no between-group difference at day 28 (P=.7804); TEWL and hydration improved in the active arm vs placebo (P=.0342; P<.0001). || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33984185/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8459234/

title: Topical palmitoyl pentapeptide provides improvement in photoaged human facial skin
raw_title: Topical palmitoyl pentapeptide improves photoaged human facial skin
authors: Robinson LR; Fitzgerald NC; Doughty DG; Dawes NC; Berge CA; Bissett DL
population: 93 Caucasian women aged 35-55
funding_or_conflicts: Authors affiliated with The Procter & Gamble Company (manufacturer).
limitations: Caucasian participants only (no Fitzpatrick IV-VI data); 3 ppm in a single vehicle.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 12-week double-blind split-face: moisturiser with 3 ppm pal-KTTKS vs the same moisturiser without it; significant reduction in wrinkles/fine lines by image analysis and expert grading; well tolerated. || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18492182/ ; https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/portal/resource/en/mdl-18492182

title: Oral and topical peptides as anti-aging agents: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
raw_title: Oral and topical peptides for skin aging: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
authors: Nukaly HY; Halawani I; Irtaza HM; Serafi MR; Alhawsawi W; Bogari HO; Ahmed FA; Alturkistani T; Alhaddad Y; Shadid A; Alharithy R; Jfri AH
population: 19 RCTs, 1,341 participants; >90% of participants in oral-peptide trials; two topical trials

notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Modest improvements in hydration, brightness and wrinkle appearance; inconsistent across ageing markers. || Verification sources: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2026.1618306/full ; https://conexiant.com/dermatology/articles/can-peptides-improve-skin-aging/

title: Topical treatment for postinflammatory hyperpigmentation: a systematic review
raw_title: Topical treatment for postinflammatory hyperpigmentation: systematic review
authors: Tan MG; Kim WB; Jo CE; Nabieva K; Kirshen C; Ortiz AE
population: 47 studies, 1,853 subjects (PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE to 29 March 2021; modified GRADE)

title: The effects of a standardized extract of Centella asiatica on postlaser resurfacing wound healing on the face: a split-face, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
raw_title: Effects of standardized Centella asiatica extract on postlaser facial wound healing: RCT
authors: Damkerngsuntorn W; Rerknimitr P; Panchaprateep R; Tangkijngamvong N; Kumtornrut C; Kerr SJ; Asawanonda P; Tantisira MH; Khemawoot P
journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine

limitations: Post-laser wound model; small effect; not evidence for everyday anti-pigmentation claims; specific standardised extract (ECa 233) not generic Centella extract.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 0.05% ECa 233 (standardised C. asiatica extract) gel vs placebo, split-face: significantly lower erythema index over follow-up (coefficient -0.03; 95% CI -0.06 to -0.0006; p=0.046); skin biophysics did not differ. || Verification sources: https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/bvsiec/resource/pt/mdl-32310680 ; https://scite.ai/authors/wilawan-damkerngsuntorn-rLe3WD

title: Enhancement of stratum corneum lipid structure improves skin barrier function and protects against irritation in adults with dry, eczema-prone skin
raw_title: Enhancement of stratum corneum lipid structure improves barrier function: RCT
authors: Danby SG; Andrew PV; Kay LJ; et al. (8 authors)
population: 34 adults with dry, eczema-prone skin (UK)
funding_or_conflicts: Funded by L'Oreal (UK) Ltd per the White Rose repository record.

title: Placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized, prospective study of a glycerol-based emollient on eczematous skin in atopic dermatitis: biophysical and clinical evaluation
raw_title: Placebo-controlled double-blind randomized study of glycerol-based emollient in atopic dermatitis
authors: Breternitz M; Kowatzki D; Langenauer M; Elsner P; Fluhr JW
population: 24 patients with atopic dermatitis (Jena; Germany)
funding_or_conflicts: One author affiliation listed with Spirig Pharma AG (product sponsor) in an indexing record; confirm in full text.
limitations: Small; clinical severity not improved vs vehicle; phototypes not reported.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 20% glycerol cream vs glycerol-free vehicle, twice daily for 4 weeks: stratum corneum hydration and barrier function improved vs placebo; no between-group difference in erythema, SCORAD or local severity. || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18025807/ ; https://karger.com/spp/article-abstract/21/1/39/295575

title: In vitro and in vivo evaluation of an emollient-rich moisturizer developed to address three critical elements of natural moisturization
raw_title: In vitro and in vivo evaluation of an emollient-rich moisturizer
authors: Draelos ZD; Nelson DB
population: In vitro epidermal model plus in vivo clinical hydration and tolerability panel
funding_or_conflicts: Second author affiliated with skinbetter science (L'Oreal USA); first author with Dermatology Consulting Services PLLC.
limitations: Finished product: cannot attribute to any single humectant; in vitro control was saline.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Multi-ingredient moisturiser evaluated for in vitro hydration/barrier biomarkers vs saline control, then in vivo hydration and tolerability. || Verification sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11966345/ ; https://onlinelibrary-wiley-com-443.webvpn.zafu.edu.cn/doi/abs/10.1111/jocd.70085

title: A double-blind study comparing the effect of glycerin and urea on dry, eczematous skin in atopic patients
raw_title: Double-blind study comparing glycerin and urea on dry eczematous skin
authors: Lodén M; Andersson AC; Anderson C; Bergbrant IM; Frödin T; Öhman H; Sandström MH; Särnhult T; Voog E; Stenberg B; Pawlik E; Preisler-Häggqvist A; Svensson Å; Lindberg M
population: 197 patients with atopic dermatitis (Sweden)
funding_or_conflicts: First author affiliated with ACO Hud AB (manufacturer) per the full-text header.
limitations: Urea arm is urea + sodium chloride (co-active); the urea arm had no own vehicle; outcomes were tolerability and dryness, not barrier biomarkers.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): 30 days: 20% glycerin cream, its base (placebo), or 4% urea + 4% sodium chloride cream. Equal effects on dryness; severe/moderate smarting 10% with glycerin vs 24% with urea-saline (p<0.0006). || Verification sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12013198/ ; https://lup.lub.lu.se/record/893447

title: The effects of common over-the-counter moisturizers on skin barrier function: a randomized, observer-blind, within-patient, controlled study

authors: Leshem YA; Wong A; McClanahan D; Simpson EL
population: Adults with atopic dermatitis (non-lesional skin)
limitations: Commercial moisturisers: not evidence for any of the 10 named emollients; underpowered.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Randomised forearm-controlled: capacitance improved on the moisturiser forearm; barrier effects small; study underpowered (recruitment fell short). || Verification sources: https://cris.tau.ac.il/en/publications/the-effects-of-common-over-the-counter-moisturizers-on-skin-barri/ ; https://www.practiceupdate.com/content/the-effects-of-common-over-the-counter-moisturizers-on-skin-barrier-function/107293/45

title: Effect of topically applied dexpanthenol on epidermal barrier function and stratum corneum hydration. Results of a human in vivo study
raw_title: Effect of topically applied dexpanthenol on epidermal barrier function: placebo-controlled human study
authors: Gehring W; Gloor M
population: Human volunteers (Karlsruhe; Germany)
limitations: Short (7 days); concentration and sample size not confirmed from abstract; healthy-skin model.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled: dexpanthenol in two lipophilic vehicles for 7 days improved stratum corneum hydration and reduced TEWL, both statistically different from vehicle. || Verification sources: https://www.thieme-connect.de/products/ejournals/pdf/10.1055/s-0031-1300268.pdf ; https://www.sigmaaldrich.com/AT/de/tech-docs/paper/383759

title: Vegetable butters and oils as therapeutically and cosmetically active ingredients for dermal use: a review of clinical studies
raw_title: Vegetable butters and oils as dermal ingredients: clinical studies review
authors: Poljšak N; Kočevar Glavač N
population: 27 clinical studies covering 17 oils: almond, argan, avocado, borage, coconut, evening primrose, kukui, marula, mustard, neem, olive, rapeseed, sacha inchi, safflower, shea butter, soybean, sunflower
limitations: Covers only shea, coconut, argan, marula, safflower and sunflower among the database's butters/oils; it does NOT cover cocoa, mango, kokum, cupuacu, murumuru, illipe, sal, Allanblackia, Pentadesma, jojoba, rosehip, moringa seed, camellia or baobab.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Oils high in oleic acid and low in linoleic acid may further damage the stratum corneum in inflamed skin; linoleic-rich oils may be more barrier-compatible. || Verification sources: https://doaj.org/article/5fd652beacfa44f899a3b40ab0fa0f62 ; https://ebusca.uv.mx/Record/pubmed-9083541

title: Effect of olive and sunflower seed oil on the adult skin barrier: implications for neonatal skin care
raw_title: Effect of olive and sunflower seed oil on the adult skin barrier
authors: Danby SG; AlEnezi T; Sultan A; Lavender T; Chittock J; Brown K; Cork MJ
population: 19 adult volunteers with and without a history of atopic dermatitis, two randomised forearm-controlled studies
limitations: Small mechanistic study; neat oils on forearm; sunflower oil grade (linoleic content) matters.
notes: Key result (abstract-level, 2026-11-25): Six drops twice daily for 4-5 weeks: olive oil significantly reduced stratum corneum integrity and induced mild erythema; sunflower seed oil preserved integrity, caused no erythema and improved hydration. || Verification sources: https://research.lstmed.ac.uk/en/publications/effect-of-olive-and-sunflower-seed-oil-on-the-adult-skin-barrier--2/ ; https://www.peeref.com/works/14401712
